title: The two birds on one tree — one eats, one watches (3.1)
hook: two birds share one tree: one pecks at the sweet fruit, the other just watches, and the Mundaka says they're both you

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bow. Om the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the target. Your line was like the arrow, become one with it.
screen: `LIKE THE ARROW, BECOME ONE WITH IT.`

segments.voice: Late at night: the third episode, the fourth cookie, the same feed scrolled twice. And sometimes, for a second, another part seems to sit a little above it all, noticing. Huh. Look at me. That part doesn't scold, exactly. It doesn't even stop you. It just sees. The Mundaka's third chapter opens with a picture of exactly that. It's older than the Upanishad itself. A tree, and two birds sitting in it.
screen: `THE THIRD EPISODE. THE FOURTH COOKIE.` → `A PART OF YOU, NOTICING.` → `A TREE, AND TWO BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. Dva suparna sayuja sakhaya. Two birds, close companions, always together, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit. The other, not eating, looks on. Commentators read the tree as the body, and the life lived in it. The bird that eats is the self as we usually know it, tasting every fruit, sweet and bitter, pleasure and pain, hungry for the next. The bird that watches doesn't eat at all. It isn't hungry. It just shines there, looking on. Then the next verse tells the story. On that same tree, the eating bird sinks down, confused, and grieves, feeling helpless. But when it sees the other, the Lord, content, and sees that one's greatness, its grief is gone. The eating bird doesn't have to fly to another tree. The watcher was on the same branch the whole time. This verse wasn't new when the Mundaka used it. It comes from the Rig Veda, from a hymn of riddles, and the Shvetashvatara Upanishad quotes it too. Here the schools of Vedanta part ways, honestly. Advaita teachers read the two birds as one self seen two ways: the watcher is who the eater really is. Madhva's Dvaita school reads them as forever two, the soul and God, close companions who never merge. Ramanuja's school reads them as two, inseparably joined, the soul as part of God's body, with God as its inner self. All of them keep the comfort of the verse. The eater isn't alone.
screen: `TWO BIRDS, CLOSE COMPANIONS, ONE TREE.` · `ONE EATS THE SWEET FRUIT.` · `THE OTHER, NOT EATING, LOOKS ON.` · `SEEING THE WATCHER, GRIEF ENDS.` · then, large: `DVA SUPARNA.`

segments.voice: Let the eating bird be busy, thoughts, wants, a little itch, a plan for later, and notice that something sees the pecking without eating or hurrying. Rest with that one for a breath. When you get caught up again, just look up, the way the eating bird looked up and saw its companion on the same branch.
Suparna, a bird of fine wings. In the Mundaka, two birds sit on one tree: one eats the sweet fruit and grieves; the other looks on, content; and seeing it, the first is freed from grief.
Your line: the one who watches. Tomorrow, three words beneath a nation's emblem. That's day four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: The two-birds verse is chanted in Vedic recitation, and Advaita, Dvaita and Vishishtadvaita teachers each explain the relation between the two birds in their own way.

original.note: Sanskrit dvā suparṇā, two birds (literally, two of fine wings): Mundaka 3.1.1, from Rig Veda 1.164.20.

chat.says: In that two-birds verse, how does the eating bird's grief end?
options: It sees the other bird, the Lord, content, and its grief is gone.
It flies off to another tree, where the fruit is sweeter.
It stops eating forever, and starves its hunger away.
chat.meaning: On the same tree the eating bird grieves, helpless; when it sees the other, the Lord, content, and his greatness, its grief is gone.
